text.title: Framework Major Upgrade Inventory Worked Examples
text.summary: One complete inventory for a Django 4.2 to 5.0 step on a billing API, with a note on every non-obvious value, and one bad inventory (a 3.2 to 5.0 jump built from a blog post) showing what the validator and the reviewer reject.

section.title: Scenario
section.p: Acme's billing API runs Django 4.2.11 on Python 3.11 and PostgreSQL 15. The team wants Django 5.0 before 4.2 leaves extended support. The suite has 1,900 tests; form rendering is covered only by view-level assertions on status codes. Two third-party packages depend on Django: Django REST framework and django-polymorphic.

example.title: Django 4.2 to 5.0, one step
example.note: `major_gap` is 1 and 4.2 is the last 4.x minor, so `release_notes_covered` holds only the 5.0 notes; a 4.0 to 5.0 path would list 4.1 and 4.2 too (r-fmui-one-major-step-per-inventory, r-fmui-breaking-change-cited-to-vendor).

The deprecation run on 4.2.11 with `-W error` produced 3 distinct warnings; two of them are entries here with `from_deprecation_run = true` and counts read from the log, the third was a duplicate of `bc-uslugify-usc-removed` from a second module (r-fmui-deprecation-warnings-as-errors).

`bc-form-rendering-div` did not fire as a warning because a changed default template is not a deprecation; it came from the release notes. Its 14 call sites run in production requests, so `blast_radius` is 28 (count x 2), and since only status codes are tested it is `runtime_no_test` with a snapshot characterisation test linked (r-fmui-call-site-count-per-change, r-fmui-risk-scored-on-two-axes).

`django-upgrade` is a complete, documented transform for the `USE_L10N` removal, so the entry is `codemod` with a 6-line dry-run diff; the form rendering change has no transform and is `manual` (r-fmui-codemod-coverage-classified).

`bc-index-together-removed` stays in the inventory as `not_affected` with the ripgrep pattern that proved zero hits; next year's 5.0 to 5.1 inventory starts from that (r-fmui-call-site-count-per-change).

django-polymorphic has no 5.0-compatible release, so it is a blocker with a `replace` plan and a linked spike; it heads the rendered risk matrix above every breaking change (r-fmui-dependent-package-compatibility).
Both runtime prerequisites are met in every environment, so neither is a blocker; they are listed anyway so the reviewer can see the check was made (r-fmui-runtime-prerequisites-listed).
`review.status` is `ready_for_review` with Kim named; the agent did not open the branch. Approval, `approved_on` and the branch are Kim's (human checkpoint).

example.title: What the validator and the reviewer reject
example.note: Validator output: `$.framework.major_gap: must equal 1, got 2`, `$.deprecation_run.every_warning_has_an_entry: must equal True, got False`, `$.release_notes_covered: 0 items, minItems=1`, `$.breaking_changes[0].risk.characterisation_test: missing required field`, `$.breaking_changes[0].status: must equal 'not_affected', got 'affected'`, `$.breaking_changes[0].codemod: missing required field`, `$.dependent_packages[0].blocker: must equal True, got False`, `$.runtime_prerequisites[0].upgrade_plan: missing required field`, `$.review.upgrade_branch_opened_by_agent: must equal False, got True`, `$.review.reviewer: missing required field`, `$.review.approved_on: missing required field`.

What the reviewer sees beyond the validator: the citation is a blog post, not the Django release notes, so the map is from memory by another name (r-fmui-breaking-change-cited-to-vendor); `pytest` without `-W error` is not a deprecation run (r-fmui-deprecation-warnings-as-errors); `blast_radius` 28 with zero call sites is a number typed in, not computed (r-fmui-risk-scored-on-two-axes); production on Python 3.8 makes the language upgrade a separate project that has to precede this one (r-fmui-runtime-prerequisites-listed).
